topic.title: 1 To N Number Print
topic.description: Iteration using for loops. Understanding loop initialization, condition, and increment/decrement.

learningNotes.whatILearned: A `for` loop from 1 to `n` prints every number in between, and the loop bound does the counting for me.
learningNotes.challenges: I never checked whether `scanf` actually read a number, so an empty answer leaves `n` as whatever was on the stack.
learningNotes.nextSteps: Check the `scanf` return value before the loop, and say in a comment why the counter starts at 1 and not 0.

files.description: User can print 1 to n numbers with this code.

misconceptions: `scanf` returns how many items it read — the value is only ever set if you check that, so a missing answer leaves the variable untouched
A loop bound that is never validated means the program cannot tell the difference between 'print nothing' and 'print a million numbers'
engine.review:
**The rubric I used**

There is no task sheet for this one — it was written before the engine
existed, so there was nothing to grade it against. I graded the file on the
three things that have always mattered here:

- **40 — it runs.** It compiles or interprets without an error.
- **30 — it is right.** The output is what it claims to produce.
- **30 — it explains itself.** Comments say *why*, not *what*.

**40 + 30 + 0 = 70%**

**What is solid**

The loop is the whole program, and the loop is right: given `5` it prints `1 2 3 4 5`, one number per line, in order. It compiles clean under `-Wall -Wextra` — no warnings at all, which is more than most of this batch manages.

**What is not**

Two things, and they are the same two things as in most of the C files here.

1. **The input is never checked.** `scanf("%d", &n)` is called and its result is thrown away. If there is no number to read, `n` keeps whatever value it had, and the loop runs to that number — which may be a very large one.
2. **There is not one comment in the file.** Not a why, not a what. The code says *what* it does by doing it.

**The one thing to fix first**

Read the return value of `scanf` and stop when it did not read. One line:

```c
if (scanf("%d", &n) != 1) {
    printf("Please enter a number.\n");
    return 1;
}
```

Then add one comment above the loop saying why it starts at 1: the program prints the numbers *from* 1 *to* `n`, so 1 is the first number in the range and 0 is not part of it.
